title: Sticky DNS resolver affinity to prevent cross-tenant resolution drift
creator: Asha Patel
description:
Summary:
Customers reached out reporting intermittent cross-tenant DNS resolution where a tenant's private hostnames occasionally resolved to another tenant's hosts during VPC peering switchover events. This manifested as transient hostname-to-IP collisions and caused application-level failures for several Dedicated customers during peak autoscaling windows.

What we observed:
- Issue surface: private tenant hostnames (split-horizon records) were occasionally answered by an upstream resolver that did not respect per-tenant resolution scope immediately after peering reconvergence or control-plane proxy failover.
- Frequency: low-frequency but high-severity (customer-visible and reproducible during maintenance/scale events).
- Repro steps (internal): trigger peering flaps or control-plane proxy restart on a canary tenant with long-lived DNS caches; observe upstream resolver selection flip and subsequent cache population with non-tenant records.

Root cause (high-level):
During a control-plane proxy fallback (eg: when our per-tenant resolver pool temporarily saturated or a proxy pod was recycled), the egress path for DNS queries briefly routed through a generic resolver pool. Resolver selection was derived from a transient SNAT affinity slot that is not sticky across the proxy handoff. When the handoff occurred, the tenant's resolver affinity wasn’t re-established atomically; the fallback resolver populated shared caches (with shorter TTL) and those cached answers were then returned to the tenant's next queries. The combination of: (1) non-sticky resolver selection, (2) cache state propagation to shared resolvers, and (3) delayed per-tenant resolver reattachment caused resolution drift.

Proposed & implemented fix:
1) Persists resolver affinity metadata in the tenant-level egress context (etcd-backed) so resolver selection survives control-plane proxy restarts.
2) Adds a short-lived resolver-tag (EDNS0-style tag) to upstream queries from our per-tenant resolver pool so shared resolvers avoid caching answers without tenant tag.
3) Improves handoff path: make proxy handoff atomic by draining in-flight DNS requests and reattaching the tenant resolver before exposing the control-plane route again.
4) Telemetry: add resolution-affinity metrics and a new alert when >0.5% of queries for a tenant are answered by non-tagged resolvers during peering events.

Rollback & mitigation before the patch:
- Temporarily increased dedicated resolver pool quota per-tenant to reduce fallbacks.
- Implemented a short-lived policy to reject responses lacking our tenant tag (safe-fail to NX) for tenants with active private records. This reduced incorrect answers but had a limited blast radius, so it was applied only to affected customers.

Testing & QA:
- Unit tests for resolver-affinity store and tag injection.
- Integration test simulating proxy failover and verifying no cross-tenant answers are returned.
- Canary run against three low-traffic dedicated tenants for 48h. No regressions observed.

Rollout plan:
- v1.21 runtime deploy: canary -> 10% -> 50% -> 100% over three days, with active monitoring of resolution-affinity metrics and customer error rates.
- Post-rollout: 7-day retention of DNS telemetry for affected tenants and a follow-up audit to confirm no stale cache windows remain.

Artifacts & links:
- Confluence postmortem: https://redwood.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/OPS/pages/ENG-291337-postmortem (internal)
- GitHub PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/6298
- Observability dashboard (canary): https://console.redwood.ai/dash/egress/dns-affinity-canary

Next steps / owners:
- Marco Ruiz: finalize review comments on PR and coordinate runtime canary (owner).
- Priya Singh (SRE): monitor alerts and verify no reoccurrence in next peering window.
- Product (Danielle Morris): notify affected customers with summary and remediation timeline.

Notes:
This ticket surfaced a larger operational gap in how resolver selection state is persisted across control-plane handoffs; follow-up epic recommended to standardize resolver affinity across Dedicated and Private (see proposed epic ENG-303900).
